Ready or Not is one of those games that I went into expecting to have a good time, but I honestly ended up enjoying it way more than I expected. There is something about this game that just feels satisfying to play. It isn't your typical run-and-gun shooter where you sprint into a room, unload your entire magazine, and move on to the next area. Ready or Not actually makes you slow down, pay attention, and think about what you're doing.

And somehow, that makes every successful mission feel so much better.

The biggest thing I love about Ready or Not is the atmosphere. The game does an incredible job of making you feel like you're actually walking into dangerous situations where you have no idea what is waiting around the next corner. Every hallway, doorway, and dark room feels like it could turn into a disaster within seconds.

You never completely feel safe.

That tension is a huge part of what makes the game so fun.

The Gameplay Feels Really Good

The gunplay is probably one of my favorite parts of the game. Weapons have weight to them, and shooting doesn't feel like you're just clicking a button to make an enemy fall over. There is a real sense of impact when you fire your weapon.

Even moving around feels different from a lot of other shooters. You're not constantly flying around the map at ridiculous speeds. You're moving through environments carefully, checking corners, watching doors, and trying to figure out what you're dealing with.

I also really like how the game gives you different ways to approach situations.

You can go in aggressively, but you can also try to control the situation and arrest suspects instead of immediately shooting them. Using things like flashbangs, pepper spray, tasers, and other equipment gives you more options during a mission.

That variety keeps the gameplay from getting boring.

One mission might have you carefully clearing a building room by room, while another can completely fall apart in a matter of seconds because you opened the wrong door.

And when you finally finish a difficult mission with your entire team alive, it feels really good.

The Levels Are One of the Best Parts

Another thing I really enjoyed is how different the maps feel from one another.

The game doesn't just give you the same building over and over again with different enemies placed inside. A lot of the maps have their own atmosphere, layout, and personality.

Neon Tomb

Neon Tomb is a great example of this.

The environment immediately gives you a completely different feeling compared to some of the other missions. The lighting, colors, and overall atmosphere make the map feel almost surreal at times.

But underneath all of that, you're still playing Ready or Not, so you have that constant feeling that something could go horribly wrong.

I really like maps like this because they show how much atmosphere matters in this game. You're not just clearing rooms because the game told you to. You're actually paying attention to the environment and trying to understand what kind of situation you're walking into.

There are moments where you're moving through an area and everything seems quiet, and that's almost worse than having enemies shooting at you.

Because you know something is probably waiting for you.

Valley of the Dolls

Valley of the Dolls is another mission that really stood out to me.

The map has such an unsettling atmosphere, and it does a great job of making you feel uncomfortable without constantly relying on cheap jumpscares.

The environment itself tells you that something isn't right.

Walking through the house and clearing each room creates this slow-building tension where you're constantly wondering what's going to happen next. You have to check rooms carefully, watch your angles, and make sure you're not putting yourself or your teammates into a terrible position.

And when you finally get through the mission, there's a genuine sense of relief.

That's something Ready or Not does extremely well.

Every Door Feels Like a Gamble

One of my favorite things about the game is honestly something as simple as opening a door.

In most shooters, opening a door is basically nothing.

In Ready or Not, opening a door can be one of the most stressful parts of the entire mission.

Is someone behind it?

Is it trapped?

Is there a civilian inside?

Is there a suspect waiting with a gun?

Is the room completely empty?

You don't know.

And that's what makes it so much fun.

You start developing your own habits as you play. You start checking underneath doors, listening for sounds, using your equipment, and communicating with your team before going inside.

The game rewards you for being careful, but it also makes you feel like you have to be careful.

The AI Can Make Things Crazy

The unpredictable situations are another huge reason I enjoyed the game.

You can have a plan going into a mission and everything can be going perfectly. Then suddenly someone runs around a corner, a suspect starts shooting, a civilian gets caught in the middle of everything, and your entire plan falls apart.

Sometimes those moments are frustrating, but honestly, they're also some of the funniest and most memorable moments.

You never really know exactly how a mission is going to play out.

That's especially fun when you're playing with friends.

A simple mission can turn into complete chaos because somebody accidentally opens the wrong door or forgets to check a corner.

And somehow, those are usually the moments you end up talking about afterward.

Playing With Friends Makes It Even Better

While Ready or Not is enjoyable on its own, playing with friends makes the game even more fun.

Having a group of people actually communicate and work together can make you feel like you're part of a real team.

One person can watch one hallway while another checks a room. Someone can use a shield while another person covers them. You can decide who goes through the door first and who watches the rear.

When everyone is actually working together, the game feels fantastic.

And then, of course, you have the missions where nobody communicates and everything immediately goes wrong.

Those are fun too, just for completely different reasons.

It Isn't Trying to Be Call of Duty

I think one of the reasons Ready or Not works so well is because it isn't trying to be another fast-paced arcade shooter.

It has its own identity.

The game wants you to slow down.

It wants you to think.

It wants you to be nervous about what's behind the next door.

And I think that's exactly what makes it stand out.

There is something incredibly satisfying about clearing an entire building and realizing that you made it through without completely losing control of the situation.

Even something as simple as successfully arresting a suspect can feel rewarding because you know you could have handled the situation differently.

The Atmosphere Is Incredible

The sound design also deserves a lot of credit.

Hearing footsteps somewhere nearby, distant gunfire, shouting, doors opening, or your teammates communicating with each other all adds to the tension.

Sometimes the quiet moments are the best.

You're standing outside a room, your team is lined up behind you, and you're just sitting there wondering what's on the other side.

Then the door opens.

Everything happens at once.

That's Ready or Not at its best.

Why I Keep Coming Back

The biggest compliment I can give Ready or Not is that I keep wanting to play another mission.

Even after finishing a level, I can think about how I could have handled certain situations differently.

Maybe I should have checked a different room first.

Maybe I should have used a flashbang.

Maybe I should have brought different equipment.

Maybe I should have been more careful.

That replayability is a huge part of what makes the game enjoyable.

You're not just replaying a mission because you have to. You're replaying it because you want to do better

I've played Ready or Not for quite a while now, and honestly, I have a pretty mixed opinion on it.
When this game is good, it's REALLY good. The atmosphere is probably one of the best things about it. The sound design, the environments, the gunshots, the way suspects react, and just slowly clearing a building with your team can be insanely immersive. It actually makes you feel like you need to think before entering a room instead of just running around and shooting everything.
The gunplay is also really satisfying. Weapons feel powerful and fights can be over extremely quickly, which I think fits the game perfectly. You actually have to be careful because making one stupid decision can get you killed. Using flashbangs, wedges, shields, checking corners and communicating with your teammates all actually feel useful.
Playing with friends is where I think the game really shines. When everyone is communicating and actually playing tactically, clearing a building feels amazing. You can spend a good amount of time planning what you're going to do, breach a room, deal with the suspects and move through the building together. Those moments are what make the game worth playing for me.
But the game definitely has problems.
The AI can be incredibly frustrating. Sometimes suspects behave realistically and make the game feel tense, and other times they can feel completely random. You can get killed by someone you didn't even know was there, or have an enemy make a decision that just doesn't make much sense. The friendly AI isn't perfect either, especially when you're playing alone.
Some missions can also feel more frustrating than challenging. There are times where you feel like you played perfectly and still get punished because of something you couldn't realistically predict. The game definitely expects you to learn from your mistakes, but sometimes it feels like the mistake wasn't really yours.
I also wouldn't recommend this game to someone who wants a fast-paced shooter. The game can be VERY slow, especially when you're playing properly. Sometimes you'll spend several minutes carefully checking rooms and hallways without much happening. Personally, I like that, but I can definitely see why some people would find it boring.
The game also isn't perfect when it comes to replayability. Once you've played certain missions multiple times, you start learning the layouts and situations, although the randomness of suspects and objectives helps keep things somewhat fresh.
Despite all of that, I still think Ready or Not is worth buying if you enjoy tactical shooters. It's not a perfect game, and I think some people give it too much praise while ignoring its problems, but there's really nothing else quite like it when you get a good squad together.
I'd say it's one of those games where your enjoyment depends heavily on who you're playing with and what you're expecting from it.
If you want realistic-ish SWAT gameplay, slow tactical clearing, intense firefights and a game that punishes you for being careless, you'll probably have a great time.
If you want something fast, casual and easy to pick up, I'd stay away.
Overall: 8/10.

**Ready or Not Review**

Ready or Not is one of those games that can be incredibly immersive when everything comes together, but also frustrating when the AI doesn't cooperate.

Coming from games like Arma, I really enjoy the slower, tactical approach. Clearing rooms, communicating with your team, dealing with civilians, and actually thinking before opening fire makes every situation feel tense.

One thing I especially appreciate is how **heavy taking a life feels**. I don't really enjoy killing people in games, and Ready or Not makes you think twice before pulling the trigger. The goal isn't to rack up kills—it's to get everyone home alive. Having to identify threats, surrendering suspects, and trying to use less-lethal options makes the game feel much more meaningful than a typical FPS.

My biggest issue is the AI. Suspects can sometimes react unrealistically fast or behave inconsistently, which can make deaths feel frustrating rather than like a mistake you made.

Still, when the game works, it's incredibly immersive. Slowly clearing a building with your team, not knowing what's behind the next door, is something most shooters can't replicate.

**8/10.** Great atmosphere, tactical gameplay, and genuinely tense encounters. The AI holds it back, but it's one of the few shooters where I actually feel like **every life matters**.

I was enjoying the first couple of missions and was a little confused by the amount of negative reviews on this game, but now that I'm getting later into the "campaign", I have to stop and leave a bad review too.

The NPCs are bad, but not as bad as like Arma 3, just unable to throw a grenade through an open doorway 50% of the time bad. The tactics and equipment are outdated and basic for real life operations, but none of that is my main gripe. Funny enough, the pre-mission briefings are what upset me the most while writing this. It is clear they spent zero time on them, yet it's what dictates my entire approach and strategy for the whole mission. I don't know how many calls in real life go from a possible single, wanted armed suspect to an entire heavily armed militia once you arrive, but it happens just about every mission to the point, I feel better off ignoring all of the briefings as they have mislead me more often then not. What prompted this negative review, was a mission where there are TWO armed suspects according to the official briefing, but one quick glance at the 911 calls and images, shows a civilian reported, and an image, clearly showing THREE armed suspects. I guess whoever wrote the briefing couldn't have been bothered enough to look at what was being placed in the rest of the file (at least this file had images and calls to correct the briefing, which cannot be said about the rest). After starting the mission, I was moving my team at about 2x my usual speed through the building, as we were warned of a possible active device in the briefing. Well, ten or so odd minutes go by and everything was going to plan, and I'd say about 75% of the building was cleared and a device was already defused, when dispatch says over the radio that another device timer was almost down to zero and to hurry up... No estimated time left, no warning of this timer beforehand when we arrived or entered the building, just a "hurry up, the device is about to go off!" Then, about twenty seconds later, it goes off, permanently eliminating every member of my crew... Like, what?! How hard would it have been to give a 5 minute warning or a countdown every minute or so with this timer that dispatch supposedly has? It's just so annoying, and makes zero sense for dispatch to hold that information from us until it's too late to act upon it. And these sort of annoying quirks happen every other mission, which leads you to repeating the mission multiple times before you understand the actual call info which you should have had at the start of briefing.

Anyway, some other complaints:
The censorship is just as bizarre as stated in other reviews. They have no problem showing certain things that easily make my stomach turn and I'm frankly shocked could even be in a video game, yet they censored mundane things that aren't nearly half as disturbing as the stuff they left uncensored.

The maps are very restrictive, not allowing you to come around the majority of structures to enter from more logical/advantageous positions, or to get solid sniper spots on windows. Talk about windows, you can't order your units to watch a window like they do doorways, so any maps where the suspects can see you through a window, you're instantly at a massive disadvantage over the enemy NPCs, and end up entirely responsible for covering them. One might even think you would also be able to enter through some of these windows, but that idea is laughable once you've played, and realized how extremely basic the physics and movement are this game. Every wall is apparently made of concrete, I don't even think you can prone, let alone slide or doing anything besides bobble around at two miles per hour.

Some of the basic modern SWAT tools are missing like: Drones, K9s, bombsquad gear, first aid kits, thermal imaging, smoke grenades, etc.

The outfit and character customization options are extremely limited, and the few clothing items they do have in the game, tend to clip through certain armor and belt variants, and don't work well together.

As someone who tries to "roleplay" out the campaign, I don't like the way they restart missions from the very beginning after you fail. I understand having an option to do this if you're trying to 100% the game, but it again, makes very little sense for you to clear half the building, make a mistake, then rather than starting where you left off and live with the consequences of your mistake, having a director yell "CUT!", and then redo everything like if you were filming a scene for a tv show or something.

Summary:
Overall, this game isn't that bad of a little SWAT commander simulator thing, especially if you get it on sale for over 50% off like I did, and I'm excited to try out the new mission editor to make some actually believable scenarios. Just go into it, knowing that the briefings are complete baloney and you won't rage nearly as much as I did, haha. However, I can understand now, why the long term supporters of this game would be cross with the state of it after all of these years. The game is still missing some of the absolute basics, and it seems very rushed and unpolished for this late into development.

P.S. It does run at a solid 30+ FPS on high settings, with 90% 4K resolution on my lower end system (specs attached) for those interested. Also, if you're running it on older hardware too, make sure you launch the Direct X11 version, or you're going to suffer through an extra two minutes or so of load time before each mission on X12, as the game attempts to load the entire level before you spawn in.

This game appealed to me for the first few dozens hours I played it, thanks to its brilliant story.
After that, I started playing online, and things have only gotten worse from that point.

MULTIPLAYER - COMMUNITY
First, the community is very toxic. This is a tactical game, but over 90% of people play it like cow boys, Call-of-Duty style, while a single bullet can get you killed instantly. When hosting a game, you'll often start a mission with a few people, and a few minutes later, when they've all gotten killed due to poor positioning (everyone loves to sit in front of door openings and expose themselves to enemy fire), poor tactical play and poor decisions, they just leave the game, probably frustrated, to go on another server, so as not to feel embarrassed by their performance. I know that, because if they happen to come back a few minutes later through the matchmaking system, they leave immediately, ashamed of how they suck.

RoN is not only tactical, it's also a game supposed to be played as a team, because every human player is on your team. However, players will just blow doors open while you wanted to take out the enemies stealthily, and of course, they'll do that when you're not ready, and when one or two of their teammates is in front of the door, exposing them to enemy fire. Feels more often like a one-for-all than efficient teamwork.

So, basically, most players have an IQ of 50, and just want to show you how good they are, until they get killed 30 seconds after the start of the mission, from a very stupid and avoidable mistake. They then ragequit, and you have to go back to the headquarters to assemble a new team (because mutliplayer is not made to played alone, right?).
I know this doesn't come from me, because I communicate a lot with my mic, give a lot of advice on the game mechanics, on tactical positioning, CQB, etc. Also, I'm chill, and even though I'm hosting, I'm not trying to command the team. As long as the team has a good lead, i don't care whether it's me or not, so even when not trying to be the boss, people still do as they please, spread out and play as if they were alone.

I've spent around 200 hours playing online (I had this game on another platform so my total playtime is not higher than Steam shows), so what I'm talking about is unfortunately not a few exceptions, but a general rule, though there are still a few good players from time to time.
Also, I've made it a habit to give the choice to the players in my lobby about which mission they want to do next, but most times, no one will give their opinion. It's only after you choose the mission that people complain or simply leave, while they were given the choice.

Now, if you don't care who you play with, and consider other players as cannon fodder, then this probably won't affect you. If you really want the tactical experience and good team work, look for another game.
And on top of all that, there are a lot of racists, xenophobes, intolerant players, and sometimes they'll even kill you from behind on purpose because they don't like your country, or because you're African or Asian. This doesn't even take into account the huge number of players that shoot hostages, most often because of a lack of vigilance, but sometimes because they think it's fun.
This it the reason I quit this game, and everytime I decided to come back to it, things were still the same, if not worse.  To me, around 90-95% of players don't understand what this game is about, and have made it a terrible experience for those who want to play like a real SWAT operator.
Unless you create your own team with people you know, you'd better have a lot of patience and understanding when hosting or joining a game, as well as lower your expectations.

MULTIPLAYER - GAMEPLAY
In multiplayer, the game is full of bugs. I have a high-end computer, cable internet, a good external mic, really everything that can make the experience as good as possible. Still, the mics often stop working entirely after a few missions, so you have to restart the game, and this affects the whole team. So, if by any chance, you were having a good time with other people, you'd better add them as friends so as to start a new lobby with them, otherwise you'll just start all over again with random people, which is like rolling the dice.
A lot of crashes also happen, which strangely almost never happen when playing solo.
The matchmaking is also very tricky. Basically, you create or enter a lobby with, as only setting, the difficulty level. Knowing that those who play in higher difficulty aren't necessarily better, more fair-play or agreeable to play with, the matchmaking is as random as can be.
So, if other players don't discourage you from playing online, the bugs or the matchmaking will.

SINGLE PLAYER
This is, surprisingly, where it gets interesting, because the AI, though not extremely bright, will in most cases be better than human players. At least, they obey, they won't go their separate way like cow boys, and unless you give the order, won't blow a door open, alerting the whole map of your presence.
Apart from that, they require a thorough management, and when giving orders, you have to look at the direction you want them to go/cover/clear/breach/etc., which, for a moment, makes you more susceptible to enemy fire, because you can't cover angles while giving orders. Your teammates will easily get shot or even killed, though, even when you're careful, because a lot of times, you have to rely on luck (and random enemy spawning) rather than skill to finish the level with zero loss on your side.
Enemy AI, however, will be more skilled than your teammates, generally, and if you happen to move in front of a window from which you can't see a damn thing, you'll have the impression the enemy was covering the few pixels where your head appeared for a millisecond, sniping you from 50 meters away. Wallbanging is also quite frequent, even if the enemy can't technically see you or know where you are. Probably AI sixth sense... The AI reaction time is also faster than most human brains, so even when stealthily approaching from behind cover an enemy turning his back on you, he can double-flip and insta-one-shot you, making even the most stoned crack-head a dangerous terminator.

This is why I don't recommend this game. The developers are lazy, and don't want to fix all of that, even though the game has been out for over 4 years. Of course, releasing DLCs is more economically viable, so making the game enoyable is not really a priority.

The main reason I'm not recommending is so that the developers do their job and fix those long-known issues and bugs, and the second reason is so that you know what you're getting into when buying the game.
However, I have to say that even though I criticize this game a lot (for good reasons), I really do like the story.
The game  doesn't show you any cinematic scene, but there is a very interesting storyline, which, if you make your research, is based on real conspiracies, like the Epstein scandals, and a lot of other real life criminal cases, that at the time of the release, were not widespread, but are now common knowledge. There are also a lot of hints you'll have to pay attention to, because this game won't spoon-feed you the whole story. If you take the time to look at the details, you'll realize all the missions are linked together, and everything is brilliantly written.
The game title's only question is not whether you're ready or not to get shot at, but if you're ready or not to step into a game that, if you're open-minded and sensitive enough, will actually punch you in the face.

I want to love this game. It's poised to be everything I've ever wanted since SWAT 3 and 4. The gameplay itself is great. The gear selection is great. The story is very interesting and rewards you for putting time into figuring out what's really going on.

And that's where the positives end.

The AI in this game is flat out broken. It starts out fine enough, though you sometimes have to wonder how the crackhead hit you with a pistol from 100m away the moment he saw a pixel of you. But that's manageable. But things ramp up and up until you're playing the last mission of the Boiling Point DLC, which is otherwise awesome, and the AI is simply absolutely impossible to beat. You have to get lucky with their positioning to even have a small chance to beat it. It's not a test of skill. It's pure luck. Suspects react in 100ms, 2.5 times a normal human reaction time, are ridiculously accurate, simply ignore shots that don't kill them half the time, not flinching at all and without any noticeably loss of accuracy.  Last time I played, I unloaded a full FiveSeven pistol magazine, with AP ammo, on a suspect's chest, that's 20 AP rounds, and he didn't even flinch. I got lucky because he got stuck on a door, giving me an opportunity to shoot him in the head. Oh, and the enemy AI also tracks you through walls.

But you have AI teammates, right? That helps, right? No, it doesn't. The teammate AI is COMPLETELY different from the suspect AI. They are not as accurate. They react slower. They routinely mismanage their own equipment, throwing flashbangs and stinger grenades at their own feet rather than near the suspect you're trying to stun. They run out of ammunition, switch to their pistol, don't shoot, switch back to their primary weapon, which is empty, so they switch back to their pistol, rinse and repeat. Sometimes they'll just decide to try and handcuff a downed suspect while actively taking fire.

I want to love this game. I really do. But I cannot recommend it as long as the suspect AI issue remains unaddressed. Which, at this point, will likely be forever, since the game has been out for almost 3 years and the developers have never even acknowledged that an issue exists.

A decent tactical SWAT shooter, though not really realistic.

The AI suspects have superhuman reaction times and can instantly headshot you or shoot you through walls, which gets in the way of the tactical gameplay. The ballistics also feel off. Suspects can take multiple rifle rounds to the chest and still keep aiming and firing with near-perfect accuracy, sometimes without even flinching, while the player can become severely impaired from a single hit.

The balance of forces is also questionable. Five SWAT operators routinely assault buildings containing 10+ armed suspects, with no meaningful external containment. Suspects can simply run into the street.

The equipment selection is actually pretty good. There is a good variety of weapons, attachments and tactical gear, and you can put together different loadouts depending on the situation.

Overall, Ready or Not is a decent tactical shooter, but calling it a realistic SWAT simulator is a stretch. The atmosphere and core gameplay are good, but the AI, damage model, ballistics and mission balance often make the game feel more like a shooter than a proper tactical SWAT sim.
